newsitem.title: JAPAN: Some jewellers sparkle despite Japan market slump.
newsitem.headline: Some jewellers sparkle despite Japan market slump.

text.p: Times are tough for many Japanese jewellers but companies offering fashionable platinum products or designs favoured by the latest teen idol can still strike success in an otherwise dull market.

Kuwayama Corp , a major jewellery manufacturer and retailer, has enjoyed a sales bonanza with a necklace similar to one worn by Namie Amuro, a young singer from Okinawa who has taken the Japanese pop scene by storm.

Kuwayama's success is in stark contrast to the more familiar story of Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten, a big Yokohama-based jeweller whose bankruptcy filing last month sent shock waves through the embattled industry.
Japanese jewellers prospered in the 1980s "bubble" of soaring asset prices and conspicuous consumption, but have been hit hard by the economic slump that began in the early 1990s.

"The jewellery business is facing its worst times in 20 years as the market shrinks, but a few popular items have saved our company," said Osamu Matsumura, a deputy general manager at Kuwayama, Japan's largest platinum jewellery maker.
Sales of Kuwayama's Omega chain surged when Amuro -- the idol of many trend-conscious youngsters -- began sporting a similar item, and Matsumura said the company now has a two-month order backlog.
While other companies make and sell Omega chains -- which have distinctively shaped links -- Matsumura attributed Kuwayama's success in large part to its focus on platinum instead of gold jewellery.

The Japanese gold jewellery sector has been battered by increased competition from Italian and Hong Kong imports, while sales of "white" platinum jewellery have soared on its image as a more sophisticated choice than yellow gold.

Japan, the world's largest consumer of platinum jewellery, saw demand stay at a record 46 tonnes last year, the same level as the previous year, according to the Platinum Guild International. Demand for gold jewellery, however, is estimated to have fallen to around 78 tonnes in 1996, down from about 87 tonnes in 1995, industry sources said.

Kuwayama, however, was forced to reduce its forecast for current profits in the year ending in March 1997 to 1.3 billion yen ($10.7 million), although it initially expected current profits to rise to a record high of 1.8 million yen ($14,800).
Current profits -- which are pre-tax and include losses or gains on investments -- in the year which ended in March 1996 were 1.48 billion yen ($12.2 million).
"Considering the slumping overall industry, we had to revise our forecasts downward," Matsumura said.
Another route to success is via well-known brand names which appeal to status-conscious buyers.

"Established brand-name jewellery is selling well. Expensive pieces priced above one million yen ($8,200), like Cartier's, recorded better sales last year than the year before despite these difficult times," said Hidetaka Kato, chairman of the Japan Jewellery Association.
Industry sources said, however, that firms lacking any special feature would collapse as the painful consolidation in the jewellery industry intensifies.

An official at a major bullion house predicted that about half of Japan's 4,000 jewellery retailers and wholesalers would disappear during the current shake-out. He and others said wholesalers would suffer most as retailers struggle to cut costs by streamlining distribution routes.

"Even the smaller Japanese retailers have recently begun dealing directly with overseas jewellery fabricators without going through wholesalers. A borderless era is certain to arrive," Kato said. ($1=121 yen)
